title: Clear Questions, Strong Descriptions
subtitle: A more challenging revision of word order, frequency, routines and personality evidence

teacherNote.summary: No new grammar topic. Use transcript-based sentence problems, make the work more difficult, include harder reading and listening within the lesson topics, add a five-exchange situational conversation, and provide a short on-platform writing task.

lessonNotes: Question word order was the main difficulty: use the question word, then the auxiliary, then the subject and the base verb.
Frequency words such as always, usually and often normally go before the main verb, but after BE. In questions, they usually come after the subject.
Present Simple describes routines and repeated actions. Present Continuous describes what is happening now or a temporary situation around now.
A personality adjective becomes clearer when you support it with a reason or example: She is active because she goes jogging every day.
The lesson briefly introduced first impressions and icebreakers. Verb + preposition and phrasal verbs were only previews for the next lesson, so they are not tested here.

grammar.title: Present Simple questions
grammar.rule: Use question word + do/does + subject + base verb. Use does with he, she and it; after does, the main verb stays in the base form.
examples: Why does your son worry about school?
How often does Kelly visit the children's home?
Do you always wake up early?

grammar.title: BE and Present Continuous questions
grammar.rule: When BE is already the verb or auxiliary, move it before the subject. Present Continuous uses question word + am/is/are + subject + verb-ing.

grammar.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammar.rule: Put always, usually, often and never before an ordinary main verb, but after BE. In a Present Simple question, put the frequency word after the subject. Usually is flexible, but the middle position is the safest choice.
examples: She often visits the children's home.
Does Kelly often visit the children's home?
I don't usually work at weekends.

grammar.title: Routine or temporary situation?
grammar.rule: Use Present Simple for repeated routines and schedules. Use Present Continuous for an action happening now or a temporary change around the present period.
examples: She goes there once a week.
She is usually a ballet dancer, but this week she is doing contemporary dance.

grammar.title: Trait + evidence
grammar.rule: Do not stop after the adjective. Add because and a complete reason, or give a concrete example that proves the description.
examples: She is strong because she can jump high.
He is arrogant because he thinks he knows more than everyone else.
My friend is easygoing. For example, she is happy to change plans.

remember: For a Present Simple question, build the frame first: question word + do/does + subject + base verb. Then add frequency and the rest of the sentence.
watchOut: Do not mix question patterns: “What is Kelly doing?” and “What does Kelly do?” are correct, but “What does Kelly doing?” is not.

reading.title: The New Trainer's First Week
reading.text:
On Monday morning, Lena arrives at Greenfield Riding Centre for her first week as an assistant trainer. She has ten years of experience with horses, but she has never worked with this team before. She wants to make a good first impression, so she arrives early, introduces herself clearly and asks where she can help. At first, Daniel, the head trainer, seems quiet and serious. Lena wonders if he is unfriendly, but she does not make a quick decision.

Daniel usually begins each morning by checking every horse and writing a short plan for the day. This week, however, he is preparing two young horses for an important competition, so the normal schedule is changing. Lena notices that he is always moving between the stable and the training area. He does not speak much because he is concentrating, not because he is arrogant. When a young rider makes a mistake, Daniel explains the problem calmly and shows her a safer method. Lena begins to see that he is patient and big-hearted, although her first impression was different.

During lunch, another colleague uses an icebreaker. She asks Lena, “What is the most surprising thing about working with horses?” Lena answers that every horse has a different personality. She describes one horse as confident because it enters new places without fear. Another horse is sensitive: it sometimes refuses to work when the rider gives unclear signals. Lena explains that calling a horse “difficult” is not enough; a trainer must give an example and look for the reason behind the behaviour.

Later, Daniel asks Lena, “How often do you train young horses?” Lena almost says, “How often you train,” but she stops and answers the question carefully. She says that she usually trains them twice a week, but this month she is working with them more often. Daniel smiles and tells her that clear communication is as important as technical experience. By Friday, Lena feels more relaxed. She has learned that a first impression can be useful, but it is not always complete. A person's repeated actions often tell a more accurate story than one short meeting.

writing.prompt: Describe one person from your family or circle of friends in 70–100 words. Use at least three personality adjectives. For each adjective, give a reason or real example. Include one frequency expression and one Present Continuous sentence about a temporary situation now.
